flawed_step: Line 0029 (together with its premise on line 0028): "The endpoints of P lie in H and are colored, say, red and blue (since H is bipartite)" / "If the length of P is odd, the other endpoint would receive the same color as the starting point, leading to a monochromatic edge when P is added."
counterexample:
Work inside the theorem's own hypotheses. Let G be the 3x3 grid graph, drawn in the plane: vertices a1,a2,a3 (top row), b1,b2,b3 (middle row), c1,c2,c3 (bottom row); horizontal edges a1a2, a2a3, b1b2, b2b3, c1c2, c2c3; vertical edges a1b1, b1c1, a2b2, b2c2, a3b3, b3c3. G is 2-connected and plane; its faces are the four 4-cycles a1a2b2b1, a2a3b3b2, b1b2c2c1, b2b3c3c2 and the outer face bounded by the 8-cycle a1 a2 a3 b3 c3 c2 c1 b1. Every face boundary is an even cycle, so G satisfies the hypothesis of Part 2.

(i) Counterexample to line 0029's inference (endpoints of different colors, ODD ear, no conflict). Take the ear decomposition that starts, as Part 2's base case instructs, from a face boundary: H = the 4-cycle a1 a2 b2 b1, 2-colored a1 = red, a2 = blue, b2 = red, b1 = blue. Add the ear P = a2 - a3 - b3 - b2, whose length is 3 (ODD) and whose endpoints a2 (blue) and b2 (red) are colored exactly as line 0028 assumes. Trace the extension: a2 = blue, so a3 = red, b3 = blue, and the next vertex must be red -- and the endpoint b2 is already red. Every edge of P joins opposite colors: a2a3 = blue-red, a3b3 = red-blue, b3b2 = blue-red. There is NO monochromatic edge. So the claim "if the length of P is odd ... leading to a monochromatic edge" is false; the parity is exactly backwards. (With distinctly colored endpoints it is an EVEN ear that would clash: e.g. an even-length path from blue a2 would end blue, colliding with red b2.)

(ii) Counterexample to line 0028's premise (endpoints of an ear need not get different colors). Take the ear decomposition H = the outer 8-cycle a1 a2 a3 b3 c3 c2 c1 b1, 2-colored a1 = red, a2 = blue, a3 = red, b3 = blue, c3 = red, c2 = blue, c1 = red, b1 = blue. Add the open ear P = a2 - b2 - c2 (endpoints a2 and c2 in H, new internal vertex b2). The endpoints are at even distance 4 along the cycle, so both are BLUE, contradicting "the endpoints ... are colored, say, red and blue (since H is bipartite)". Bipartiteness of H forces nothing about the relative colors of two arbitrary vertices. Here the ear has even length 2 and extends fine (b2 = red: edges a2b2 = blue-red, b2c2 = red-blue), which is again the opposite of the rule asserted on line 0029.

The same instance also shows why the repair attempted on lines 0031-0033 cannot work: the regions created by adding P = a2-b2-c2 to the octagon are bounded by the 6-cycles a1 a2 b2 c2 c1 b1 and a2 a3 b3 c3 c2 b2, and NEITHER is a face of G -- both are later subdivided by the ears b1b2 and b2b3. So the hypothesis "every face of G is an even cycle" simply does not apply to the intermediate region invoked on line 0031.
reasoning_summary:
Lines 0001-0009 are definitions and are unobjectionable. Lines 0010-0018 (Part 1) are correct: for a 2-connected plane graph the boundary of every face is a cycle (line 0012 cites this standard fact without proof, which is acceptable), and a cycle in a bipartite graph must have even length by the alternation argument given -- Part 1 goes through.

Part 2 is where the proof breaks. Line 0022-0025 (ear decomposition of a 2-connected graph starting from a cycle, base case an even face boundary, 2-colored) is fine. The inductive step then fails at lines 0028-0029. Line 0028 asserts, with "since H is bipartite" as its justification, that the two endpoints of the new ear P carry DIFFERENT colors; bipartiteness of H gives no such thing, and the 3x3 grid witness in the counterexample field exhibits a legitimate ear whose two endpoints are both blue. Line 0029 then asserts that an odd-length ear forces a monochromatic edge; under its own assumption of oppositely colored endpoints this is exactly backwards -- an odd path between a red and a blue endpoint extends consistently, as the explicit color trace a2(blue), a3(red), b3(blue), b2(red) shows, while it is an even-length ear that would clash. Since the whole inductive step is a case analysis built on this reversed parity rule, it establishes nothing.

Per the early-stop protocol I stop here, but I note that lines 0031-0037 do not rescue the argument: they invoke "the boundary of the new face created by adding P" and apply the hypothesis about faces of G to it, whereas that region is a face only of the intermediate subgraph H' and is generally subdivided by later ears (illustrated in the same witness). Lines 0036-0037 then merely assert that "the parity of P must match appropriately" without deriving it, so the induction is never actually carried out. (The theorem itself is true -- the standard proof shows every cycle is a symmetric difference of the face boundaries it encloses -- but this proof does not prove it.)
